idiom_name: for ... range over slice, array, map, string, channel (and int since Go 1.22)
implementation_notes: Go's enumeration message is the range clause, and it belongs to the language rather than to the collection: for i, v := range xs walks slices and arrays by index, maps by key/value pair, strings by rune, channels until close, and since Go 1.22 an integer for a counted loop. A user-defined type cannot define its own range behaviour, so custom collections expose enumeration by returning a slice or channel, or - since Go 1.23 - by handing out an iterator function. Range replaces the index loop wherever the elements themselves are wanted; keep the three-clause for where the counter is part of the algorithm.
pitfalls: range copies the element: for _, v := range xs gives a copy, so mutations must go through xs[i] (pointer element types still share the pointee).

The loop variable was shared across iterations before Go 1.22, so goroutines and closures created in the body all observed the last element; per-iteration variables (Go 1.22) fixed it, but capturing the variable deliberately to share state now fails silent expectations.
Map iteration order is deliberately randomised and a channel range ends only at close, so neither form is a deterministic sequence.

variants.name: Iterator functions (range over func)
variants.implementation_notes: Go 1.23 lets a collection expose enumeration as a value: an iterator function func(yield func(T) bool) - typed as iter.Seq[T], or iter.Seq2[K,V] for pairs - can be ranged over directly, with early exit propagated by yield returning false, and slices.Values/maps.Keys/iter.Pull bridging the standard library. This is the first way a user-defined type can be 'walked with one message' in Go; the price is a closure per invocation and a yield protocol the compiler cannot check.
pitfalls: Ignoring yield's false return keeps producing elements after the consumer stopped (and may retain memory); the iterator body must return immediately.
An iterator function is lazy: setup before the first yield runs when ranging starts, so side effects move in time and an iterator must not be reused unless it documents re-iteration.
